social.instagram_caption:
Pill or patch? For blood clots, the way you take HRT may matter.

A nationwide Danish study in The BMJ looked at women aged 50 to 69.
Oral HRT was linked to more clots in the legs or lungs.
The number headlines skip: about 1 extra clot per 1,000 women per year. Real, but small.
Patches and gels showed no overall increase in these clots.
Why? Swallowed oestrogen goes through the liver first, which is thought to boost clotting proteins. Through the skin, most of that is bypassed.
The catch: it's observational and didn't have data on weight or smoking. It shows a link, not proof.

Your own risk depends on your age, weight, smoking and any history of clots. Ask your clinician which route fits you, and don't stop or switch on your own.

Save this for your next menopause appointment and share it with someone weighing up HRT 💬

factcheck.summary:
I checked every claim against the BMJ Group press release, Medical Xpress, the BMJ DOI (it resolves), the NHS HRT page and the Neville et al. 2026 paper on PMC. All of them support the script.

- **The study:** a Danish nested case-control study of women aged 50–69 (2003–2021), published in The BMJ in September 2026, DOI 10.1136/bmj-2026-100688.
- **Oral HRT:** linked to more clots in the legs or lungs (venous thromboembolism) at any dose and for any length of use. The authors give one extra case per 1,055 women per year of oral use, so "~1 per 1,000" is a fair rounding. It is correctly presented as an absolute risk.
- **Patches, gels and other skin-applied HRT:** no general increase in clot risk.
- **Limitations:** the study had no data on body mass index (BMI) or smoking. The script mentions this and correctly calls the finding "a link, not proof".
- **Liver explanation:** the claim that swallowed oestrogen passes through the liver and raises clotting proteins is hedged, and the Neville et al. paper supports it.
- **Safety wording:** the "don't stop or switch on your own" line meets channel policy.

The only fix is a small citation error: src3's listed title is a paraphrase, not the paper's real title. The NHS page's scheduled review date (Feb 2026) has passed, but the page is live and still consistent with the script.

audio.soundNotes: I left the music as it is (multiplier 1.0), because it already sits about 14 dB under the voice, which is inside the target. I cut the SFX that stack up on each other: duplicate swoosh/whoosh pairs, the rapid run of swooshes at 7 s, 16 s and 25 s, and the burst of pops under the "~1 in 1,000" stat, where only the ding and two quieter pops remain. I also turned down a few blips and pops that were louder than about −15 dB during speech, so this serious risk topic stays clear and uncluttered. I didn't add any custom effects.
